Dermatology · published research

Eyebrow loss

A 16-person single-arm study reported higher eyebrow hair counts after LED treatment and at six-month follow-up, but there was no untreated or sham comparison.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 16-person single-arm study reported higher eyebrow hair counts after LED treatment and at six-month follow-up, but there was no untreated or sham comparison.

Summary of the Evidence

One publication reports a single-arm study of 16 women aged 60 to 74 with eyebrow loss associated with frontal fibrosing alopecia. Hair counts were measured before treatment, after ten sessions, and six months later. No comparator or independent cohort was identified. No animal or cell study directly addressed this indication.

Human and clinical evidence

After ten weekly LED sessions, total eyebrow-hair count and counts of thick and medium-thickness hairs were higher than baseline. At six months, total count remained significantly above baseline. Treatment was reported as well tolerated. Some thickness-specific counts fluctuated after treatment, so every measure did not rise continuously for every participant (Gerkowicz et al. 2021).

Without an untreated brow or sham group, natural variation, concurrent management, and measurement conditions cannot be excluded. The result concerns eyebrow loss in frontal fibrosing alopecia, not other causes of eyebrow thinning or scalp hair loss.

Animal evidence

No animal evidence was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell or ex-vivo study specifically examined this condition.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The protocol used 630-nm LED light, red visible light, at 37 J/cm² and 68 mW/cm². Sessions lasted about nine minutes weekly for ten weeks and treated the eyebrows and frontal hairline. One protocol does not establish whether other doses or schedules would yield similar changes.

Interpretation

Counts increased within this group and remained above baseline at follow-up. Without a comparator, the LED contribution is uncertain. Controlled replication in the same condition is needed.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for eyebrow hair-count change in frontal fibrosing alopecia
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The study measured hair objectively in 16 women and included a six-month follow-up, which helps describe change over time. It had no sham, untreated eyebrow, or comparison group, and there is no independent replication in the indication category. A controlled study with blinded hair counts and clearly recorded concurrent treatments would be needed to support a stronger rating.
